short_title: Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te
full_title: DEVELOPMENT BANK OF THE PHILIPPINES, REPRESENTED BY ITS GENERAL SANTOS CITY BRANCH HEAD, MARIELA LUZ T. CORTEZ, PETITIONER, VS. MANUEL TE, RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > T. Execution, Satisfaction, and Effect of Judgments (Rule 39) > 1. Immutability of Final Judgments; Exceptions
topics: Immutability of a final judgment of indirect contempt
Later (partial) compliance cannot undo a final contempt judgment
Civil vs. criminal contempt; direct vs. indirect contempt (Rule 71)
An order modifying a final judgment is void; affirming it is grave abuse of discretion
doctrine:
**A judgment finding a person guilty of indirect contempt, once final and executory, is immutable. The trial court cannot later lift it, or remove the penalties it imposed, because the contemnor has since (even partly) complied with the order he disobeyed.** Under the doctrine of finality or immutability of judgments, a final decision may no longer be modified in any respect, even to correct erroneous conclusions of fact or law. Any amendment that substantially affects it is null and void for lack of jurisdiction, as are the proceedings held for that purpose (Industrial Management International Development Corp. v. NLRC; Eusebio v. CSC, reiterated). An order that is worded as a recognition of compliance but in practice nullifies the final contempt judgment is an impermissible modification, and an appellate court that affirms it commits grave abuse of discretion.

Contempt is direct (committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct the administration of justice) or indirect (willful disobedience of the lawful process or order of the court). Contempt proceedings are sui generis. They are civil when the dominant purpose is remedial, to compel obedience to an order for the benefit of a party, and criminal when it is punitive, to vindicate the dignity and authority of the court (Lorenzo Shipping, reiterated). **Even when the contempt is civil in nature, the final judgment imposing it can no longer be disturbed.**
facts:
In Civil Case No. 347 before the RTC of Polomolok, South Cotabato, Branch 39, Manuel Te, as attorney-in-fact of the Abedin group, sued DBP to recover 131 certificates of title and 34 other proofs of ownership that the group had surrendered as security for a loan. The RTC issued a writ of replevin; DBP surrendered the documents to the sheriff, who handed them to Te. Te then moved to dismiss the case because the Abedin group had lost interest in prosecuting it. On March 2, 2004, the RTC denied the motion and ordered Te, as the group's attorney-in-fact, to surrender to the court the titles and other proofs of ownership within 30 days. It denied his motion for partial reconsideration on October 11, 2004.

Te did not surrender all the documents, so DBP filed a petition for indirect contempt on December 1, 2010. On April 16, 2014, the RTC found Te guilty and sentenced him to a fine of PHP 30,000 and imprisonment of two months "or until he duly complies" with the court's order, under Rule 71, Sections 3(b) and (d) and 7. The CA affirmed. The Supreme Court denied Te's petition (G.R. No. 225250) on September 14, 2016 and his motion for reconsideration with finality on June 18, 2018, and entry of judgment issued.

Te later filed a Manifestation of Compliance with the RTC. He claimed that he had recovered 12 out of the 131 certificates of title and 34 proofs of ownership, and that the March 2, 2004 Order was directed to the Abedin group, not to him. On July 17, 2020, the RTC deemed its orders complied with and lifted the order of contempt. It found no willful disregard of its order because the titles had already been returned to the landowners, a matter beyond Te's control, and stated that despite the finality of its judgment it could still exercise discretion on whether to impose the penalty. DBP's motion for reconsideration was denied. On October 29, 2021, the CA dismissed DBP's petition for certiorari. It held that the RTC did not modify a final judgment but only gave effect to Te's compliance, and that DBP showed no grave abuse of discretion. The CA denied reconsideration on March 16, 2022.
issues: Whether the contempt proceedings against Te were civil or criminal in nature.

Whether a final and executory judgment of indirect contempt may be lifted because of the contemnor's later compliance with the order he disobeyed, and whether the CA gravely abused its discretion in affirming the RTC order that did so.
ruling:
**1. The contempt was civil in nature.** Citing Lorenzo Shipping, the Court explained that contempt is direct or indirect, and that contempt proceedings, being sui generis, are criminal when their primary purpose is punishment (vindicating the dignity of the court) and civil when it is compensatory or remedial (enforcing compliance with an order for the benefit of a party). Te had been found guilty of indirect contempt for failing to obey the March 2, 2004 Order, and DBP filed the contempt case as a remedial measure to compel his compliance, so the proceedings were civil.

**2. No, the final judgment could not be lifted, and the CA gravely abused its discretion.** A final decision becomes immutable and may not be modified in any respect, even to correct errors of fact or law. An amendment that substantially affects it is void for lack of jurisdiction, as are the proceedings held for that purpose. In Eusebio v. CSC, the Court reversed the CA's reduction of a fine imposed in a final judgment of indirect contempt. The Court stressed that this principle is "especially vital in cases involving judgments for indirect contempt, which are punitive in nature and rendered after due process." Here, the Court itself had affirmed the contempt judgment in G.R. No. 225250. **Te's later attempt to comply "cannot operate to invalidate or undo a judgment that has long attained finality."** Although the RTC presented its order as a recognition of compliance, its practical effect was to nullify the final judgment and remove the penalties. That was an impermissible modification, and the proceedings for it were void ab initio for lack of jurisdiction; a lower court has no authority to alter a final ruling, least of all one upheld by the Supreme Court. **By affirming this patently void order, the CA acted capriciously and arbitrarily, amounting to grave abuse of discretion.**
disposition: The Petition for Review on Certiorari was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated October 29, 2021 and Resolution dated March 16, 2022 in CA-G.R. SP No. 10244-MIN, which affirmed the RTC's July 17, 2020 Order lifting the contempt, were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Te was directed to STRICTLY COMPLY with the Orders of the RTC of Polomolok, South Cotabato, Branch 39 dated March 2, 2004 and "October 11, 2014" (as written in the fallo; see notes).

bar_questions.q: The RTC found Gerry guilty of indirect contempt for refusing to deposit in court the original titles he had been ordered to surrender, and sentenced him to a fine of PHP 30,000 and imprisonment of two months or until he complies. The judgment was affirmed on appeal and became final and executory in 2022. In 2024, Gerry turned over a few of the titles and filed a manifestation of compliance, explaining that the rest were already with the landowners and beyond his control. The RTC deemed its order complied with and lifted the contempt judgment and its penalties. Was the RTC's order valid?

alac.answer: No. The order is void because it modified a final and executory judgment.
alac.legal_basis: Under the doctrine of finality or immutability of judgments, a final decision may no longer be modified in any respect, even to correct errors of fact or law, and any amendment that substantially affects it is void for lack of jurisdiction. A contemnor's later attempt to comply cannot invalidate or undo a final judgment of indirect contempt. An order that lifts the contempt and removes its penalties is an impermissible modification even if it is worded as a recognition of compliance. (Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te, G.R. No. 260664, August 18, 2025)
alac.application: The contempt judgment against Gerry became final in 2022. The RTC's 2024 order speaks of compliance, but in practice it nullifies that judgment by removing the fine and the imprisonment. Whatever Gerry's reasons for delivering only some of the titles, they could not reopen a judgment that the RTC no longer had jurisdiction to alter.
alac.conclusion: The RTC's order lifting the contempt is void because it violates the immutability of final judgments.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as above, but Gerry argues that the contempt was civil, not criminal, because the bank filed it to compel him to deliver the titles for the bank's benefit. Since the purpose of civil contempt is coercive, he says, that purpose is served once he complies, and the court may lift the penalty even after finality. (a) Is the contempt civil or criminal? (b) Does its civil character allow the court to lift the final judgment?

alac.answer: (a) It is civil contempt. (b) No. Even a civil contempt judgment, once final, cannot be lifted or modified because of later compliance.
alac.legal_basis: Contempt proceedings are sui generis. They are civil when the dominant purpose is to enforce compliance with an order for the benefit of a party, and criminal when the dominant purpose is to vindicate the dignity and authority of the court (Lorenzo Shipping Corp. v. Distribution Management Association of the Philippines). In Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te (G.R. No. 260664, August 18, 2025), the Court found the contempt civil because it was filed to ensure compliance with a court order, yet held that the final judgment could not be lifted upon the contemnor's later compliance, because doing so would violate the immutability of judgments.
alac.application: The bank sued to compel Gerry to deliver the titles for its benefit, so the contempt is civil. But the nature of the contempt does not change the effect of finality. The judgment, including its penalties, became immutable, and the RTC lost jurisdiction to alter it. Gerry's partial delivery cannot reopen it.
alac.conclusion: The contempt is civil, but the final judgment still cannot be lifted on account of Gerry's later compliance.

bar_questions.q: (a) Distinguish direct contempt from indirect contempt. (b) After the RTC lifted a final judgment of indirect contempt, the aggrieved party filed a petition for certiorari with the Court of Appeals. The CA dismissed it, reasoning that the petition merely questioned how the RTC appreciated the contemnor's compliance, which is at most an error of judgment, not grave abuse of discretion. Is the CA correct?

alac.answer: (a) Direct contempt is committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct the administration of justice; indirect contempt is willful disobedience of a lawful process or order of the court. (b) No. The RTC order is void for lack of jurisdiction, and the CA gravely abused its discretion in upholding it.
alac.legal_basis: Direct contempt is committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct him in the administration of justice; indirect or constructive contempt consists of willful disobedience of the lawful process or order of the court. Proceedings to amend a final and executory judgment are void ab initio for lack of jurisdiction, and a court that affirms such a patently void order acts with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. (Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te, G.R. No. 260664, August 18, 2025, citing Lorenzo Shipping Corp. v. Distribution Management Association of the Philippines)
alac.application: (a) Refusing to surrender documents as the court ordered is disobedience of a lawful order committed outside the court's presence, so it is indirect contempt. (b) The RTC's order is not a mere mistake in weighing compliance. By lifting a judgment that had become final, the RTC acted without jurisdiction, which is exactly the kind of defect that certiorari corrects. In refusing to annul the order and leaving it in force, the CA committed grave abuse of discretion, as the Supreme Court held in DBP v. Te.
alac.conclusion: The CA is wrong; it should have annulled the RTC order that lifted the final contempt judgment.

notes: Dates in the source text are inconsistent. The facts give the denial of Te's partial reconsideration as October 11, 2004, but the fallo directs compliance with the Orders dated March 2, 2004 and "October 11, 2014." The 2014 contempt decision refers to an "ORDER dated 4 March 2004," and the RTC's July 17, 2020 Order calls the Orders dated March 2, 2004 and "April 16, 2004" the "Contempt Order," although the contempt decision itself is dated April 16, 2014. The Court did not rule on whether Te actually had the remaining titles or whether the March 2, 2004 Order was directed to him personally; its holding rests only on the immutability of the final contempt judgment. The resolution calls the proceedings civil (remedial) in nature but also describes judgments for indirect contempt as "punitive in nature." Although a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, the case was decided on whether the CA committed grave abuse of discretion.
